text: You start with capital w. There are n projects. Project i needs at least capital i to start, and when you finish it you gain profits i. You can do at most k different projects, one after another. Return the most capital you can end with.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — capital i is only a threshold. I need that much to start, but I don't pay it. So when I finish a project, w just goes up by the profit. Is that right?
Right. Nothing is spent. Profit is pure gain.

Then that's the key fact. Profits are never negative, so w never goes down. Once a project is affordable, it stays affordable forever — the set of projects I can start only grows. Two more things. Distinct means each project at most once, right? And if nothing is affordable, I just stop early, and doing fewer than k is fine?
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n and k are up to ten to the fifth. w and each capital are up to ten to the ninth. Profits are up to ten to the fourth. The answer fits in a thirty-two-bit signed int.

Okay. With ten to the fifth for both n and k, k times n is ten to the tenth — too slow. I want about n plus k, times log n. Quick check on the example: k is two, w is zero, profits one, two, three, capital zero, one, one. With zero, only project zero is affordable. I do it, so w is one. Now projects one and two both open up. I pick the bigger profit, three, so w is four. The answer is four.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to run k rounds, and in each round scan all n projects and pick the best affordable one I haven't done. It's correct, but k times n is way too slow. Which one is best? The one with the biggest profit. More money only opens up more projects and never closes one, so greedy is safe here. This problem reminds me of a sort-and-sweep feeding a max-heap. Projects unlock in capital order, so I sort the indices by capital once and walk them with one pointer. Among the unlocked ones, I need the max profit fast — that's a max-heap of profits. Each project is pushed and popped at most once, so this is n log n plus k log n.

Here's the plan. One: sort project indices by capital. Two: in each of the k rounds, push every newly affordable profit into a max-heap. Three: if the heap is empty, stop; otherwise add the top to w and pop it. One thing worth flagging — the loop is driven by k, not by the pointer. The refill must happen every round, after w grows, because the last profit might unlock new projects. The pointer can reach n early while the heap still has good projects, so that's no reason to stop. The only early stop is an empty heap: nothing is affordable, and since w can't change, nothing ever will be. There's a trade-off: the heap stores plain profits, not indices — I never revisit a project once it's unlocked. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. I sort the indices by capital, then run k rounds. The inner while is the refill — it runs at the start of every round, after the last profit. The heap stores profits only; a priority queue of int is a max-heap by default, so the top is the biggest profit I can afford. One thing worth flagging — the push loop uses less than or equal, not less than. With a strict less than, project zero in both examples needs zero and I have zero, so it never unlocks, and both examples return zero. And the empty-heap break isn't just an early exit — without it, the next line calls top on an empty heap.

Let's dry-run the code on example one. The key row is round two. Round one only unlocked project zero, and its profit made w one. That one unit unlocks projects one and two together at the start of round two. Both go into the heap, and the max-heap gives me three, not two — so w is four. That matches. Corner cases: nothing affordable — the heap is empty in round one, so I break. K bigger than n — after the only project, the heap is empty and I break. A chain — profits one, one, capital zero, one — project one unlocks only after project zero is done, so I return two. That chain broke my first draft: it returned as soon as the heap went empty, before refilling, and got one. The fix is to refill first, then check.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is n log n plus k log n. The sort is n log n. The pointer only moves forward, so across all rounds there are at most n pushes, and at most k pops, each log n. Space is linear, for the index array and the heap. In the worst case, n and k are both ten to the fifth. That runs in about fifteen to twenty milliseconds, while the rescan-every-round version takes over twenty seconds. I also checked it against a brute force on over eighty million small cases with zero mismatches — worth it, because some buggy versions still pass both examples.
Is int safe for w? You keep adding to it.

Here, yes. The biggest legal answer is ten to the ninth plus ten to the fifth times ten to the fourth — two billion. That's still about a hundred and forty-seven million below the int max, and the problem promises the answer fits. If the limits were any bigger, I'd switch w to long long. Oh, one more thing — the whole greedy rests on w never going down. If capital were a cost I had to pay, an unlocked project could become unaffordable again. Then always taking the biggest profit would no longer be safe, and the one-pointer refill would break. That's exactly why the first thing I asked was whether capital is spent.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You asked whether capital is spent, and used w never going down to justify both the greedy and the one-pass pointer. You made the loop run on k with a refill every round, and showed with a two-project chain why returning on an empty heap before the refill is wrong. And you tested past the official examples, since buggy versions can pass them both. Good work.
